questions.question: Name the elements of the oral communication process and identify where miscommunication usually enters.
questions.solution: Sender → message (encoded) → channel → receiver (decodes) → feedback, with NOISE acting on the channel. Miscommunication typically enters at ENCODING (the sender's wording doesn't carry the intended meaning), DECODING (the receiver's assumptions differ) or through NOISE (literal sound, distraction, jargon). Feedback is the loop's repair mechanism — without it, errors persist.

questions.question: What behaviours distinguish active listening from merely waiting for your turn to speak?
questions.solution: Active listeners give attention cues (eye contact, nodding), paraphrase back ('So you're saying…'), ask clarifying questions instead of assuming, and withhold judgement until the speaker finishes. Waiting-to-speak means rehearsing your reply while the other talks — you hear words but not meaning. Paraphrasing is the testable marker: it proves decoding happened.

questions.question: Give one semantic, one psychological and one physical barrier to oral communication, with a fix for each.
questions.solution: Semantic: jargon or ambiguous words ('as soon as possible' — how soon?) → fix by defining terms and using concrete language. Psychological: prejudice or anxiety filtering what is heard → fix by checking assumptions and paraphrasing. Physical: noise, poor phone line, distance → fix by changing channel or environment. Each barrier acts at a different stage, so each needs a different repair.

questions.question: A speaker says 'I'm delighted' with crossed arms and a flat tone. Which message does the audience believe, and why?
questions.solution: The non-verbal one. Tone, posture and expression carry the emotional content of a message and are read as more honest than words — verbal and non-verbal signals in conflict make the audience trust the body. Congruence (words matching delivery) is what makes a speaker credible; a mismatch is read as insincerity.

questions.concept: Speaking to be heard — audience adaptation
questions.question: How should a talk about water conservation differ when addressed to farmers versus to schoolchildren?
questions.solution: Farmers: practical, economic framing (irrigation scheduling, crop yield, cost saving), technical vocabulary they own, examples from their fields. Schoolchildren: concrete images and stories, simple vocabulary, interactive questions. Same content, different entry point — audience analysis (what they know, what they care about) determines vocabulary, examples and appeal.

questions.concept: Group discussion — the contribution that scores
questions.question: In a group discussion, why does dominating the floor usually score LOWER than fewer, sharper interventions?
questions.solution: GDs assess listening, reasoning and team behaviour — not airtime. The strong contributor listens, builds on others' points ('Adding to what X said…'), brings evidence, and synthesises disagreements into a working position. Monopolising signals poor listening and blocks the group's thinking. Quality and relevance of turns beat quantity.

questions.question: When asked 'Tell me about a time you solved a problem', what structure makes the answer convincing?
questions.solution: STAR: Situation (brief context), Task (what you were responsible for), Action (what YOU specifically did — the longest part), Result (the measurable outcome). Interviewers want evidence of behaviour, not claims; STAR converts 'I'm a good problem-solver' into a demonstrable instance. Keeping Situation short and Result concrete is what separates strong answers.

questions.question: Why should a business call open with identification and a purpose statement within the first two sentences?
questions.solution: The phone strips away all visual context — the receiver knows nothing except the voice. Identifying yourself and your purpose immediately lets them route the call and retrieve the right information; vagueness wastes both parties' time and reads as unprofessional. State who, why, and what you need — then listen.
